object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged occurrence representing something broken, tracked through states from triage to closed.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Good, that's a firm rule. How is an incident identified? Nadia: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, format INC- followed by a sequence, never reused or deleted.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Nadia: Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: An origin record indicating monitoring (or manual) detection of a problem, identified by Alert ID from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: And an alert -- identified how? Nadia: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Identifier for an alert, issued by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that may be linked to an incident as an origin, identified by ticket number.

source_references.excerpt: Owen: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Identifier for a support ticket, from a different system/format than incident numbers.

source_references.excerpt: Owen: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact/blast radius classification of an incident, from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, one region).

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer urgency classification of an incident, from P1 to P4, based on who's affected, commitments, and SLA breach risk.

source_references.excerpt: Owen: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Which is completely different... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current status of an incident: triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, or closed.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed. ... Facilitator: Five, and an incident is in exactly one? Nadia: Exactly one at a time.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander for the duration of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Is a service owner a team or a person? Nadia: A team. Services are owned by teams.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service in the catalogue that can be affected by incidents and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Person identification is unclear - the transcript only says the commander is 'one person, named' without specifying a formal identifier (employee ID, username, etc.). Using a name as a reference mode risks non-uniqueness if two commanders share a name.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority history: both are said to change over time ('constantly' for severity) and the current value is stored on the incident while changes are recorded in a separate 'timeline' as events. The timeline/events concept is not modeled since it wasn't described with sufficient structure (fields, identifiers). Should a full history fact type be captured?

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. ... Nadia: In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status mentioned by Owen is explicitly excluded from the model per the facilitator's decision ('If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it'), but it indicates a potential future/unofficial state that stakeholders disagree about. Flagging for completeness in case business rules evolve.

source_references.excerpt: Owen: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. Nadia: That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. ... Facilitator: If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Classification of customer-caused (user-error) incidents for reliability metrics is explicitly undecided and parked for a separate stakeholder (Ravi) to decide. No object type or fact type for 'cause classification' has been modeled, per facilitator's explicit statement.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. ... Nadia: That's accurate and slightly painful.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'owner': the term is used ambiguously in practice to mean either the Incident Commander (temporary role) or the Service Owner (standing team assignment). The model disambiguates these as two distinct fact types (Incident is commanded by Person; Service is owned by Team), but the transcript notes ongoing confusion in actual usage ('who owns this?').

source_references.excerpt: Owen: And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'sev': colloquially used to mean either Severity or Priority, causing miscommunication (e.g., 'we've got a sev one'). The model keeps Severity and Priority as fully independent value types, consistent with Nadia and Owen's clarified position, but real-world usage conflates them.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.

ambiguities.description: The disjunctive mandatory 'at least one origin' constraint spans two separate fact types (Incident originates from Alert, Incident originates from Ticket). This is expressed as a single disjunctive_mandatory constraint referencing the Alert-origin fact type's Incident role, but conceptually it requires the disjunction to be evaluated jointly across both fact types; the schema representation may need to explicitly reference both fact types for full accuracy.

source_references.excerpt: There's no path to an incident that doesn't have either an alert or a customer report behind it. ... Never neither. The declare form won't let you.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate chain acyclicity/directness is stated as the intended rule but explicitly 'not enforced' in the actual system today. It's ambiguous whether this should be modeled as a hard constraint (representing intended business rule) or omitted/flagged as a soft rule given current real-world violations (two-deep chains observed).

source_references.excerpt: Kit: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... Kit: That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.
